incidents.title: App servers open a connection per request
incidents.brief: Each HTTP request opens a new Postgres connection and p99 login time on the database climbs.
incidents.constraint: The database max_connections is 200 and there are 40 app pods.
incidents.question: What is the first fix?

choices.label: Bound pool
choices.resultBody: Reuse a bounded connection pool per process instead of connecting per request.

choices.label: Raise max conn
choices.resultBody: Raising max_connections lets more sessions in, but 40 pods still open a fresh TCP, TLS and auth handshake per request; Postgres forks a backend per login and CPU pins at 100%.

choices.label: Connect per request
choices.resultBody: Opening a new connection on every retry doubles the logins Postgres must fork and authenticate, and sessions slam into the 200 max_connections limit within seconds.

hints: Sessions to the database are unbounded.
Handshake cost is the tax.
Reuse a bounded pool.

incidents.title: Postgres refuses logins after payroll scale-out
incidents.brief: Ledgerly's API autoscaled to 50 pods for payroll day. Each pod's pool opens 50 connections, so Postgres sees 2,500 attempts against max_connections 500 and rejects new sessions.
incidents.constraint: Peak load needs only ~300 busy connections, and the 64 GB primary cannot host thousands of backends.
incidents.question: How do you stop scale-out from exhausting the database?

choices.label: Set per-pod pool to max_connections divided by max pods

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Cheap and immediate, but pod count and pool size are now coupled.

choices.resultBody: Pools drop to 8 per pod and HPA max is pinned at 60, so the fleet can never hold more than 480 sessions; peak needs ~300, so p95 falls to 90 ms. Cost: pool size and replica count are now coupled, and every scaling change must redo that division.

choices.label: Raise max_connections to 3,000 on the primary
choices.resultBody: Postgres now accepts all 2,500 sessions, but each is a forked backend with its own memory and snapshot overhead; CPU pins at 99% on context switches and p95 gets worse, reaching 3.1 s.

choices.label: Point half the pods at a new read replica
choices.resultBody: Payroll traffic is 80% writes, so the 25 pods sent to the read-only replica fail their INSERTs and retry against the primary, which still sees 1,250 connection attempts for 500 slots.

hints: Multiply two numbers in the brief and compare the result with a third.
The database limit is fixed; the per-pod pool size is a config value.
Work backwards from max_connections to what each pod may hold at maximum scale.

incidents.title: Bigger pools made checkout slower
incidents.brief: Carthop saw pool waits and raised each of its 12 pods from 10 to 60 connections. Now 720 sessions run at once on a 16-vCPU Postgres; throughput fell from 9k to 6k queries/s and p95 went from 30 ms to 900 ms.
incidents.constraint: The database instance size is fixed until next quarter.
incidents.question: How many connections should actually be doing work?

choices.label: Shrink to 4 per pod, about 3x the DB's cores

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Queueing moves to the app, where it's cheap; bursts wait a few ms for a connection.

choices.resultBody: 48 active sessions keep all 16 cores busy without thrashing on context switches and lock queues; throughput climbs back to 9.5k queries/s and p95 to 35 ms. Cost: bursts now wait briefly in each pod's pool queue instead of inside Postgres.

choices.label: Grow the pools again to 100 per pod
choices.resultBody: More connections mean more backends competing for CPU, buffer-pool latches and row locks; throughput drops again to 4.8k queries/s and p95 passes 1.5 s.

choices.label: Put PgBouncer in session mode in front
choices.resultBody: In session mode every client still pins one server connection for its whole life, so Postgres still sees 720 busy sessions; nothing changes except an extra ~0.3 ms per query.

hints: The database got slower when you gave it more work to do at once.
16 cores can only run about 16 queries at the same instant.
Let excess requests wait in the app, not inside the database.

incidents.title: Orders stall while connections wait on a shipping API
incidents.brief: Parcelbay's order flow opens a transaction, locks the stock row, calls a shipping-rate API (800 ms), then commits. Each connection is held 850 ms instead of 10 ms, pools sit at 100%, and 19% of orders time out.
incidents.constraint: The shipping API can't be made faster; it's a third party.
incidents.question: How do you stop connections waiting on something that isn't the database?

choices.label: Fetch the rate first, then run a short transaction

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Short transactions; a few orders fail the stock re-check.

choices.resultBody: The rate is fetched before any connection is borrowed; the lock-check-insert-commit transaction then takes 10 ms, pool use falls to 20% and timeouts to 0.1%. Cost: stock can change during the 800 ms call, so the transaction re-checks it and rejects about 0.2% of orders.

choices.label: Grow each pod's pool from 30 to 120
choices.resultTitle: More idle transactions, more lock waits
choices.resultBody: Four times the connections hold four times the row locks; orders for popular items now queue on the stock-row lock instead of the pool, and p95 rises to 7 s with 22% timeouts.

choices.label: Kill transactions idle for more than 500 ms
choices.resultBody: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout now terminates any session waiting on the 800 ms shipping call, so the commit fails on a closed connection and 58% of orders error out.

hints: The database is at 18% CPU. It isn't the slow part.
What is each connection doing during those 800 ms?
Borrow the connection only for the part that talks to the database.

incidents.title: Flash sale Lambdas can't log in to Postgres
incidents.brief: A TicketDrop flash sale pushes Lambda concurrency from 40 to 900 in one minute. Each execution environment opens its own Postgres connection, and RDS rejects logins past max_connections 400.
incidents.constraint: The sale must stay open: throttling the checkout function is not allowed.
incidents.question: What lets 900 concurrent functions share 400 database connections?

choices.label: Route functions through RDS Proxy's shared connection pool

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Multiplexes many short-lived callers onto a warm pool, for a proxy bill and ~1-2 ms per query.

choices.resultBody: RDS Proxy keeps ~300 warm connections and lends one per transaction, so 900 functions multiplex onto them and the login storm stops. Cost: about 1-2 ms extra per query, a per-vCPU proxy bill, and session state (SET, temp tables) pins a connection and defeats multiplexing.

choices.label: Open a pool of 5 connections inside each function
choices.resultBody: A pool inside a Lambda serves one invocation at a time, so 900 environments now try to hold 4,500 connections against the 400 limit and login failures more than double.

choices.label: Cap checkout at 300 reserved concurrency
choices.resultBody: Postgres recovers, but 600 of 900 concurrent checkouts get TooManyRequestsException during the drop, which the constraint forbids; fans refresh and roughly double inbound traffic.

hints: Count the callers and count the connection slots.
A function instance can't share its connections with its neighbours on its own.
Something long-lived has to own the connections on the functions' behalf.

incidents.title: Every deploy causes a 90-second login storm
incidents.brief: Quillpad rolls 40 pods, 8 at once. New pods start with empty pools and instantly take 900 req/s each; handshakes time out and retry, so Postgres sees 900 TLS + SCRAM logins in 5 s. CPU hits 95%, p95 4 s.
incidents.constraint: Deploys happen 12 times a day and can't be paused.
incidents.question: How does a new pod join without a connection stampede?

choices.label: Prefill 20 connections before readiness passes

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Smooth rollouts; each deploy step is ~15 s slower.

choices.resultBody: Each pod opens its 20 connections at a steady pace during startup and reports ready only after the pool is full, so the load balancer never sends traffic to a cold pod. Logins spread over 30 s, DB CPU stays at 60%. Cost: each rollout step takes about 15 s longer.

choices.label: Raise the pool's connect timeout to 30 s
choices.resultTitle: Requests wait longer for the same storm
choices.resultBody: Fewer requests fail outright, but 160 logins still land in the same second as each batch of pods starts; requests on new pods now wait up to 30 s, and p95 during deploys rises to 9 s.

choices.label: Turn off TLS to the database to speed up logins
choices.resultBody: Connection setup drops from ~60 ms to ~25 ms of DB CPU, so the storm is shorter, but SCRAM and backend forks still spike CPU to 85%, and plaintext database traffic breaks the SOC 2 control the next day.

hints: The pain only lasts while new pods are coming up.
A new Postgres connection costs a TLS handshake, auth, and a process fork.
Do the expensive part before the pod takes real traffic.

incidents.title: Month-end reports lock out checkout
incidents.brief: Ledgerline's finance reports and checkout share one 20-connection pool per pod. At month-end, 30-second report queries hold 18 of 20 connections, checkouts wait 8 s for the other 2, and 27% fail.
incidents.constraint: Finance needs reports from live data on the primary today.
incidents.question: How do you stop one workload from taking every connection?

choices.label: Split into a 3-connection report pool and a checkout pool

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Workloads isolated; heavy reports are throttled and run longer.

choices.resultBody: Reports can now hold at most 3 connections per pod and queue behind each other, while checkout keeps its own 17. Checkout wait drops to 2 ms and failures to 0.1%. Cost: month-end reports take about 6x longer to finish.

choices.label: Double the shared pool to 40 per pod
choices.resultTitle: Reports grow into the new space
choices.resultBody: Finance's job runner launches reports as fast as connections free up, so 36 of 40 are soon held by scans; DB CPU climbs to 97% and checkout waits get worse at 11 s.

choices.label: Set a 5 s statement timeout on every query
choices.resultBody: Report queries are cancelled at 5 s, so connections free up and checkout failures fall to 3%, but every finance report now errors out and they retry in a loop, keeping DB CPU at 70%.

hints: Two very different workloads draw from one bucket.
The slow one naturally ends up holding most of the connections.
Give each workload a limit it can't exceed.

incidents.title: Writes fail for 12 minutes after a 30-second failover
incidents.brief: Bidly's Aurora writer failed over in 30 s, but each pod's pool kept 40 open sockets to the old writer, now a read-only replica. 'Cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction' continued for 12 minutes, until maxLifetime recycled them.
incidents.constraint: Failovers happen about twice a month during patching.
incidents.question: How should the pool react when its connections point at the wrong node?

choices.label: Evict the whole pool on a read-only error, reconnect

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Fast recovery after failover; a brief login burst on every node.

choices.resultBody: The first read-only or connection error marks every pooled connection stale; the pool reconnects via the cluster endpoint with a 5 s DNS TTL and writes recover about 35 s after failover. Cost: a short reconnect burst of 40 logins per pod.

choices.label: Retry failed writes three times with backoff
choices.resultTitle: Retries reuse the same stale sockets
choices.resultBody: Each retry borrows another connection from the same pool, which also points at the old writer; errors stay at 60% for 12 minutes, and now each failed bid takes 2 s longer.

choices.label: Restart every app pod after each failover
choices.resultTitle: Works, but only as fast as a human
choices.resultBody: Fresh pods connect to the new writer, but someone has to notice and run the rollout; this time it took 7 minutes, and 60 pods restarting at once caused a 90 s login storm.

hints: The database recovered quickly. The app didn't.
Pooled sockets remember which host they connected to.
Treat a read-only error as proof the whole pool is out of date.

incidents.title: Checkout threads queue for a DB connection
incidents.brief: Cartwheel runs 6 pods at 600 req/s each. Every request holds a connection for 40 ms, but each pod's pool has 10 connections, and 180 of 200 servlet threads sit blocked waiting.
incidents.constraint: Postgres max_connections is 300, and the database is idling at 45% CPU.
incidents.question: What pool size should each pod run?

choices.label: Size pools from arrival rate times hold time, ~30 each

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Right-sized pool; must be recomputed when traffic or query time changes.

choices.resultBody: Little's law: 600 req/s x 0.04 s = ~24 connections busy per pod, so a pool of 30 leaves headroom and 6 x 30 = 180 stays under 300. Pool waits vanish and p95 drops to 70 ms. Cost: DB CPU rises to ~60%, and the math must be redone when pods or query times change.

choices.label: Match each pool to all 200 servlet threads
choices.resultBody: Six pods x 200 connections asks Postgres for 1,200 sessions; only about 1.5 pods' worth get in, the rest hit 'too many clients', and errors more than triple.

choices.label: Cut servlet threads to 10 to match the pool
choices.resultTitle: Queue moved to the load balancer
choices.resultBody: No thread blocks now, but 10 concurrent requests at 40 ms caps each pod at ~250 req/s against 600 arriving, so the LB queue grows and p95 hits 3 s.

hints: The pool is too small, but by how much?
Connections in use = arrivals per second x seconds each one is held.
Check your number against max_connections divided by the pod count.

incidents.title: Tenants query each other's schemas
incidents.brief: Plotline runs PgBouncer in transaction mode: 1,200 app clients share 100 server connections. Code runs SET search_path once per request, and 3% of queries land in another tenant's schema.
incidents.constraint: Postgres can afford about 100 server connections; session pooling would need 1,200.
incidents.question: How do you stop tenant state leaking across pooled connections?

choices.label: Use SET LOCAL inside each request's explicit transaction

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Keeps 12:1 multiplexing; every request must run in an explicit transaction.

choices.resultBody: SET LOCAL scopes search_path to the transaction PgBouncer lends out, so it resets at COMMIT and can't leak, while 1,200 clients still share 100 server connections. Cost: each request needs BEGIN/COMMIT, and other session features (advisory locks, LISTEN, WITH HOLD cursors) stay off-limits.

choices.label: Switch PgBouncer to session pooling mode
choices.resultBody: Session mode stops the leak but pins one server connection per client for its whole life, so 1,100 clients wait in PgBouncer's queue and p95 jumps from 45 ms to 4 s.

choices.label: Force RESET ALL after every transaction in PgBouncer
choices.resultBody: With server_reset_query_always on, RESET ALL runs between the SET and the next statement, so queries stop leaking but now land in the public schema; 'relation does not exist' errors jump to 3,000/s.

hints: The leak only happens because of the proxy's current mode.
In this mode a server connection belongs to a client for one transaction only.
Make the setting's lifetime match the length of the connection loan.

incidents.title: Webhook sender can't assign an address
incidents.brief: Hookrelay posts 2,500 webhooks/s from one pod to a partner API. Each call builds a new HTTPS client and closes it, leaving sockets in TIME_WAIT for 60 s. With 28k ephemeral ports, connect() fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL for 41% of deliveries.
incidents.constraint: The partner allows at most 200 new TLS connections per second from you.
incidents.question: How do you send 2,500 req/s without burning a port per request?

choices.label: Reuse keep-alive connections from one shared HTTP agent

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Far fewer handshakes; long-lived connections need idle and max-age limits.

choices.resultBody: A single agent keeps up to 80 keep-alive TLS connections to the partner; at ~25 ms per call, about 64 of them carry 2,500 req/s. TIME_WAIT sockets fall to near zero and handshake CPU disappears. Cost: the agent must cap per-host sockets and recycle ones the partner closes.

choices.label: Widen the ephemeral port range to 1024-65535
choices.resultTitle: Twice the ports, still too few
choices.resultBody: 64k ports divided by a 60 s TIME_WAIT allows about 1,070 new connections per second, less than half the 2,500 needed; failures fall to 18% and handshake CPU stays at 88%.

choices.label: Scale the sender out to 4 pods
choices.resultBody: Four source IPs give enough ports, but 2,500 new TLS handshakes per second is 12x the partner's 200/s limit; it returns 429 on 70% of connection attempts.

hints: The error is about local ports, not the partner being down.
Every closed connection keeps its port busy for a minute.
Stop opening a new connection for every request.

incidents.title: Requests wait 60 s for a connection nobody will use
incidents.brief: Rentwise's 20-connection pool per pod runs dry when a search query slows. Its acquire timeout is 60 s, but the load balancer gives up at 30 s, so 180 of 200 Tomcat threads wait for connections for clients who already left.
incidents.constraint: Listing pages must stay up even when search queries slow down.
incidents.question: What should a request do when no connection is free?

choices.label: Cap connection wait at 300 ms and return 503

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Bounded waiting; a few requests are rejected quickly instead of slowly.

choices.resultBody: A request that can't get a connection in 300 ms now fails fast with 503 and Retry-After, freeing its thread; pages that don't need the slow query keep serving. Errors fall to 4% and p95 to 400 ms. Cost: some users see a quick retry message at peak.

choices.label: Raise Tomcat's thread limit to 800
choices.resultBody: The extra threads join the queue for the same 20 connections; 760 now wait, heap grows by 600 MB, and a GC pause of 4 s makes even health checks fail.

choices.label: Raise the pool from 20 to 80 connections
choices.resultBody: More connections let four times as many slow search queries run at once; DB CPU climbs to 99%, every query slows further, and threads are soon waiting on 80 busy connections.

hints: Compare the pool's wait time with the load balancer's timeout.
A request whose client already left is pure waste.
Waiting for a connection needs its own short deadline.

incidents.title: First requests after every quiet hour hang for minutes
incidents.brief: Tidepool's app reaches RDS through a NAT gateway that silently drops TCP flows idle for 350 s. The pool keeps idle connections for 30 minutes, so after lulls, queries on dead sockets hang until TCP gives up, 15 minutes later.
incidents.constraint: The network team can't change the NAT gateway's idle timeout.
incidents.question: How do you keep the pool from handing out connections the network already dropped?

choices.label: Retire idle connections after 4 minutes, below 350 s

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: No stale sockets; occasional reconnects after quiet periods.

choices.resultBody: The pool closes connections idle for 240 s, well under the NAT's 350 s, and keeps a TCP keepalive at 60 s on the rest, so no dead socket is ever handed out. Hangs drop to 0. Cost: after a lull the first few requests pay a ~40 ms reconnect.

choices.label: Run a warm-up query from cron at 07:55
choices.resultBody: The cron query itself hangs on the first dead socket, and the lull at 13:00-14:00 is just as long as the night; users still hit 15-minute hangs twice a day.

choices.label: Test each connection with SELECT 1 before use
choices.resultBody: Validation spots dead sockets, but only after its 5 s timeout, so after a lull a request may burn 5 s per stale connection it borrows, and every healthy query now pays an extra round trip.

hints: It only happens after the app has been quiet for a while.
Something between the app and the DB forgets idle flows without telling either side.
Compare the pool's idle timeout with the network's.

incidents.title: Random SSL errors since enabling preload
incidents.brief: Menuly turned on gunicorn preload_app to cut startup memory. The SQLAlchemy engine is created at import in the master, then 8 workers fork and share its pooled sockets: 9% of queries fail with 'decryption failed or bad record mac'.
incidents.constraint: Preload saves 1.2 GB per host and the team wants to keep it.
incidents.question: Where must each worker's connection pool be created?

choices.label: Dispose and rebuild the engine in each worker after fork

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Correct per-process pools; more total DB connections.

choices.resultBody: A post_fork hook calls engine.dispose(close=False) so every worker opens its own connections; no two processes write to one TLS stream any more and errors drop to 0. Cost: 8 workers x 5 connections means 40 per host instead of 5.

choices.label: Wrap every query in a threading lock
choices.resultTitle: A lock no other process can see
choices.resultBody: A threading lock only serializes threads inside one process; the 8 forked workers still interleave bytes on the same inherited sockets, so errors stay at 9% and throughput drops.

choices.label: Retry any query that raises an SSL error
choices.resultTitle: Retries hit the same shared sockets
choices.resultBody: Retries often land on another shared socket and fail again; worse, a few INSERTs had reached Postgres before the error, so retried orders are written twice.

hints: It started exactly when the processes began sharing memory at startup.
After fork, parent and children hold copies of the same open file descriptors.
A connection must belong to exactly one process.

incidents.title: p99 spikes to 3 s every 30 minutes on the dot
incidents.brief: After Tripnest restarted all 300 Go pods at 09:00, every pgx pool connection shares one start time and a 30-minute max lifetime. At 09:30, 10:00 and 10:30, 15,000 connections expire and reconnect within 2 seconds.
incidents.constraint: Connections must still recycle so new replicas get traffic after scale-out.
incidents.question: How do you keep connection recycling from happening all at once?

choices.label: Add a 10-minute random jitter to max connection lifetime

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Smooth, continuous recycling; lifetimes vary by up to 10 minutes.

choices.resultBody: With MaxConnLifetimeJitter at 10 minutes, each connection expires at a random point between 30 and 40 minutes, so about 25 reconnects per second happen continuously instead of 15,000 in two seconds. p95 stays at 40 ms. Cost: nothing noticeable.

choices.label: Disable max lifetime so connections never expire
choices.resultBody: The half-hour storms stop, but connections now live for days: after scaling to a new reader they stay pinned to old ones, and one reader runs at 90% while the new one idles.

choices.label: Raise max lifetime from 30 to 120 minutes
choices.resultBody: All connections still share one start time, so they still expire together; the 15,000-reconnect spike now arrives every 2 hours instead of every 30 minutes.

hints: The spikes are perfectly periodic.
Every connection in the fleet was born in the same minute.
Give each connection a slightly different expiry time.

incidents.title: Pool drains 40 minutes after every restart
incidents.brief: Since Tuesday's deploy, Bookly's 20-connection pool per pod empties about 40 minutes after start. The new card-decline path returns early without releasing its connection, so requests wait 30 s.
incidents.constraint: Postgres shows 20 idle sessions per pod, and restarts only buy another 40 minutes.
incidents.question: What stops connections from disappearing?

choices.label: Release in finally blocks and turn on leak detection

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Fixes the root cause; requires a sweep of every early-return path.

choices.resultBody: try/finally (or a with/using block) returns the connection on the decline path too, and a 10 s leakDetectionThreshold logs the stack of any future borrower that holds on. Usage settles at 6 of 20. Cost: a code sweep of every early return, plus log noise from slow but legitimate queries.

choices.label: Double the pool to 40 connections per pod
choices.resultBody: Latency recovers for now, but the same leak drains 40 connections in about 80 minutes instead of 40, and Postgres carries twice as many orphaned idle sessions per pod.

choices.label: Cut the pool checkout timeout from 30 s to 2 s
choices.resultBody: Requests now fail after 2 s instead of hanging for 30 s, which frees threads, but all 20 connections are still leaked, so nearly every booking still errors.

hints: The connections aren't lost in Postgres; the app still owns them.
Look at the code path that shipped in Tuesday's deploy.
Every borrow needs a return on every exit, including error paths.
